summary: Contains the requirements that a AAA service must support to help provide Mobile IP services. It is informational.

eli5.summary: When a phone moves between networks, the new network must check who it is and keep count of use. This lists what is needed.

subtitle: Requirements for AAA infrastructure to support mobile nodes roaming between networks.

tldr.problem: Mobile IP enables devices to move between networks while maintaining connectivity, but when a mobile device visits a foreign network, that network needs to authenticate the device, determine what services it can use, and bill its home provider—requiring AAA (Authentication, Authorization, Accounting) infrastructure.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a basic AAA model with local and home authorities, security requirements for Mobile IP registration, key distribution, and a broker model to scale trust relationships across multiple domains.
tldr.outcome: The requirements in this RFC guided the design of AAA protocols like Diameter and influenced the Mobile IP protocol extensions that support AAA integration.

facts.label: Key participants
facts.value: Mobile node, attendant (FA/DHCP), local AAA, home AAA, optional broker

facts.label: Key distribution
facts.value: AAA provides MN-HA, MN-FA, and HA-FA keys during registration

today: RFC 2977 remains the definitive requirements document for AAA support of Mobile IP. While not obsoleted, the protocol landscape has evolved: Diameter (RFC 6733) largely supersedes RADIUS for AAA, and Mobile IPv6 has modified some requirements due to the absence of foreign agents. The broker model and scalability principles established here remain relevant for modern roaming and multi-domain deployments.

sections.title: Introduction to Mobile IP AAA
sections.content:
Mobile IP is a technology that allows a network node to migrate from its home network to other networks, maintaining the same address and connectivity. When a mobile node (MN) moves to a foreign network, an agent in that network (the attendant) may require the mobile node to provide credentials before granting access. The attendant typically does not know how to validate those credentials directly; instead, it contacts a local authority (AAAL) which may consult the mobile node's home authority (AAAH) to authenticate the credentials and determine what services the mobile node may use.

The RFC identifies functional and performance requirements that Mobile IP places on AAA protocols. Unlike document RFC 2881, which models a generic NAS, this RFC focuses specifically on the requirements that arise from mobile devices roaming across domain boundaries and the need for efficient, secure authentication and key distribution.
sections.eli5: When you travel to another country, the local network can't check your passport itself, so they ask your home country to verify who you are and say whether you're allowed to be there.

sections.title: Basic AAA Model and Security Associations
sections.content:
The RFC establishes a three-party model: a client (mobile node), an attendant (foreign agent or address allocation entity), and AAA servers in both the local and home domains. Three critical security associations are required: (1) between the client and its home authority (AAAH), since the client belongs to the home domain; (2) between AAAL and AAAH, to allow them to trust each other's authentication results and authorization decisions; (3) between the attendant and the local authority (AAAL), so the attendant knows it is safe to allocate resources.

The RFC notes that requiring bilateral security relationships between every pair of AAA servers is not scalable. For example, in a roaming scenario with many service providers, each provider would need to establish relationships with every other provider. This leads to a quadratic growth in trust relationships, addressed later through a broker model.
sections.eli5: Three relationships must be secure: you must trust your home provider, the local network must trust your home provider, and the front desk must trust the local management.

sections.title: AAA Protocol Roaming Requirements
sections.content:
Based on operational experience with RADIUS in roaming networks, the RFC specifies requirements for any AAA protocol supporting Mobile IP. The protocol must provide reliable transport with hop-by-hop retransmission and failover, since latency between distant AAA servers could cause Mobile IP timeouts. Acknowledgments should be piggybacked in AAA messages to reduce round-trip count.

The protocol must support message integrity, identity authentication, and replay protection on a hop-by-hop basis. It should transport digital certificates to minimize round-trips during AAA transactions. Real-time accounting must be supported with timestamps. Inter-domain accounting should be possible both through bilateral arrangements and via broker AAA servers that provide clearinghouse and reconciliation functions between serving and home networks.
sections.eli5: Messages must arrive reliably and quickly. Messages must be proven genuine and not replayed. The system must count what was used and report it fairly between networks.

sections.title: Mobile IP-Specific AAA Functions
sections.content:
Mobile IP registration requires specific AAA functions. The AAA servers must enable (re)authentication for Mobile IP registration, authorize the mobile node to use resources, and initiate accounting for service utilization. These tasks benefit from being handled together by AAA servers because they often happen simultaneously and need access to the same data.

Critically, any Mobile IP data sent through AAA servers must be considered opaque to the AAA servers. Authorization data must be derived by the attendant (foreign agent) from information supplied by the mobile node. This keeps the AAA system from becoming entangled in Mobile IP protocol details. The AAA servers must be able to perform key distribution during initial Mobile IP registration, creating or identifying security associations between the mobile node and home agent, between mobile node and foreign agent, and between home and foreign agents, allowing subsequent registrations to proceed without further AAA involvement.
sections.eli5: During the first registration, the AAA system sets up the secret keys the device needs for later logins. It checks who the device is, decides what it can do, and gets everything ready so the next time is faster.

sections.title: Broker Model for Scalability
sections.content:
To solve the quadratic growth problem in trust relationships, the RFC introduces a broker model. A broker AAA server (AAAB) sits between local and home authorities, allowing them to cooperate without direct bilateral relationships. Instead of every provider trusting every other provider, they only need to trust the broker, and the broker validates transactions on behalf of all.

The broker model requires end-to-end security so that the home and local domains can verify signatures even though a message passes through the broker. The broker must be able to forward encrypted data so the home domain can send sensitive information (like registration keys) without the broker seeing it. The RFC notes that multiple layers of brokers must be supported for highly diverse service provider networks.
sections.eli5: Instead of every network trusting every other network, they all trust a neutral referee. The referee makes sure transactions are fair without learning the secret details.

sections.title: IP Connectivity and Dynamic Address Allocation
sections.content:
The RFC requires that AAA servers be able to obtain or coordinate the allocation of a suitable IP address for the mobile node upon request. Mobile nodes should be able to identify themselves by a Network Access Identifier (NAI) of the form "user@realm" rather than requiring preconfiguration of home agents and addresses. The home AAA server (AAAH) should be able to select a home agent and coordinate allocation of a home address, simplifying mobile node configuration.

The RFC also addresses scenarios where a local AAA server (AAAL) can allocate a local home agent in the local domain for roaming users who don't need to maintain connectivity to their actual home network. This reduces latency for registrations and simplifies firewall traversal. Additionally, local payments (cash, credit card) processed by the local AAA server may eliminate the need to contact the home authority.
sections.eli5: The device can say who it is using just a name (user@home.provider). The AAA system assigns a temporary local address and sets up a local relay point so registration is fast.
